steps.body: Unit rates with fractions show up anywhere two quantities compare — laps around a track, cups in a recipe, minutes on a clock. The flip-and-multiply rule works the same way every time.
Pace, on two lines at once.

widget.prompt: A car covers 12 km per litre. Set the top line to show the distance on 3 litres.
widget.successFeedback: 36 km. The two lines are locked together — the ratio is the same at every step, which is exactly what makes the relationship proportional.
widget.lowFeedback: Too short for 3 litres at 12 km per litre.
widget.highFeedback: Too far for 3 litres at 12 km per litre.

predict.prompt: The lines mark litres and km in lockstep. Three ticks along, the km line reads…
predict.reveal: Each tick is one litre worth 12 km, so three ticks is 3 × 12 = 36. The two lines stretch together — that lockstep IS proportionality. Writing 12 + 3 mixes the litre scale into the km scale.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents unit rate context.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for unit rate context must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines unit rate context.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

widget.prompt: A runner covers 7/8 lap in 7/16 hour. What is the unit rate in laps per hour?

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies the fractions directly. Flip and multiply: (7/8) × (16/7) = 2.

steps.body: In a recipe, the unit rate tells you how much of one ingredient per single unit of another — useful for scaling a recipe up or down correctly.

widget.prompt: A recipe uses 1/6 cup of oil for every 1/3 cup of water. What is the unit rate in cups of oil per cup of water?

options.feedback: That flips the wrong fraction. (1/6) ÷ (1/3) = 1/2, not 2.
That multiplies the fractions directly instead of dividing. (1/6) ÷ (1/3) = 1/2.

steps.body: The units always match the question: "laps per hour," "cups per cup," "miles per minute" — the unit rate's name tells you which quantity goes on top.

widget.prompt: A machine fills 2/5 cup in 1/5 minute. What is the unit rate in cups per minute?

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies the fractions directly. Flip and multiply: (2/5) × 5 = 2.

widget.prompt: A recipe uses 1/4 cup of milk for every 1/2 cup of flour. What is the unit rate in cups of milk per cup of flour?

options.feedback: That flips the wrong fraction. (1/4) ÷ (1/2) = 1/2, not 2.
That multiplies directly instead of dividing. (1/4) ÷ (1/2) = 1/2.

widget.prompt: A cyclist covers 2/5 lap in 1/5 hour. What is the unit rate in laps per hour?

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies the fractions directly. Flip and multiply: (2/5) × 5 = 2.

widget.prompt: A recipe uses 3/10 cup of sugar for every 3/20 cup of butter. What is the unit rate in cups of sugar per cup of butter?

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies the fractions directly. Flip and multiply: (3/10) × (20/3) = 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: (3/10) ÷ (3/20) = 2 cups of sugar per cup of butter.

hints: Flip the second fraction and multiply: 3/10 × 20/3.

steps.body: Unit rates with fractions work the same way in any context — laps, recipes, or time.
takeaways: The flip-and-multiply rule applies to any two compared quantities.
The unit rate's name tells you which quantity is "per" the other.
Recipes, laps, and rates all use the same fraction-division method.

concept.body: Unit rates with fractions work the same in any context. Flip the second fraction and multiply: laps, cups, or time, it's always (a/b) × (d/c).

widget.prompt: A skater covers 5/6 lap in 5/12 hour. What is the unit rate in laps per hour?

commonErrors.feedback: Flip and multiply instead of multiplying directly: 2.
